2.4. Electrochemical Performance of Full Cell
We also have tested the low-temperature performance of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL in the cathode material of SIBs. Na $_{3}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{3}$ was selected as the cathode with Na metal anode to assemble a coin cell. Rate performance of Na||NVP coupled with both electrolytes were evaluated. NVP paired with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL achieves a capacity of up to 74.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while it exclusively remains 60.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2, as demonstrated in Figures S22–S24 (Supporting Information). Surprisingly, it can operate normally at LT, and specifically preserve a capacity of 79.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ at $-40$ °C, which is equivalent to 80.0% of the capacity at 25 °C in Figure S25 (Supporting Information). This indicates that temperature-adaptive electrolytes are not only compatible with NVP, but can also upgrade the rate performance and low-temperature performance of NVP cathode.

To further verify the feasibility of electrolytes in SIBs, the coin full cell with NVP cathode and pre-cycled HC anode was assembled and subjected to rate performance testing at 25 °C. It displays that the full cell coupled with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can still retain a capacity of 71.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while the cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 can only bestow a capacity of 52.3 mAh g $^{-1}$ in Figure 6a. Additionally, the performance of the full cell was evaluated at -40 °C and it was manifested that the full cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can preserve 64.8% of its capacity at 25 °C in Figure 6b. After 50 cycles of 0.1 C (10 mA g $^{-1}$ ) at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 95.7%, and then after 50 cycles of 0.1 C at -40 °C, the capacity retention rate was 92.8%, as shown in Figure 6c. To test the practical application of electrolytes, a piece pouch cell (45 mAh) was assembled for cycling testing in Figure 6d and Figure S26 (Supporting Information). After cycling 100 cycles at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 86.7%. Then, the pouch cell was cycled 100 cycles at -30 °C, and the capacity retention rate was 92.43% in Figure 6e. Therefore, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL electrolyte with a temperature-adaptive solvent structure holds great potential in the practical application of SIBs.

source_refs.raw_quote: As the most commonly used electrolyte for SIBs, a PC-based electrolyte composed of 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ -PC/FEC was used as the control (hereafter referred to as PC) [42,43]. Similarly, the proposed carboxylate ester-based electrolytes in this work are composed of MP, FEC, and NaPF $_{6}$ . Firstly, the influence of concentration on electrochemical stability and ionic conductivity of the electrolyte was investigated, and as shown in Fig. S1(a), the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte with 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ is significantly higher than that of the electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ . Moreover, the MP-based electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ has better electrochemical stability (Fig. S1(b)), therefore 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ -MP/FEC was selected for research, which will be referred to as MP in the following. The redox reaction activities of isolated solvents and sodium salt of MP and PC-based electrolytes are investigated with frontier molecular orbital theory, involving the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy levels (Fig. 1(a)). The LUMO/HOMO energy level of MP is close to PC, which indicates MP has considerable oxidation/reduction stability compared to PC. In addition, the HOMO level of FEC is lower than that of the other solvents, indicating the stronger capability of the free fluorinated carbonate solvent against oxidation.

source_refs.raw_quote:
2.5. Toward Practical Viability
To further validate the practicality of the NTM electrolyte, full cells with NVP cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes were constructed, operating within the voltage range of 2.0–3.6 V (Figure 5a). The NVP||HC full cell, without any presodiation treatment, exhibits a high specific capacity of 88.0 mA h g $^{-1}$ and excellent cycling stability over 100 cycles at 50 mA g $^{-1}$ , maintaining an impressive capacity retention of 84.9% in the NTM electrolyte. This retention markedly surpasses that of the conventional NP electrolyte (51.9%), as illustrated in Figure 5b,c. Furthermore, the full cell utilizing the NTM electrolyte demonstrates superior rate capability, delivering reversible capacities of 87.2, 82.0, 79.1, 77.0, 71.9, and 68.1 mA h g $^{-1}$ at 20, 50, 80, 100, 200, and 300 mA g $^{-1}$ , respectively (Figure 5d). The charge–discharge curves exhibit minimal polarization even at elevated rates (Figure S32, Supporting Information). In addition, the overall electrical performance of the NTM electrolyte is better than that of the NED (NP-EC/DMC) electrolyte (Figure S33, Supporting Information). Notably, the NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 500 cycles at a high current of 200 mA g $^{-1}$ (Figure S34, Supporting Information). Self-discharge behavior was further evaluated in the NVP||HC full-cell system. The results display that the NP electrolyte system retains 72.8% of its discharge capacity after 48 h of rest (based on 4th cycle). In contrast, the NTM system exhibits a smaller capacity loss, achieving a retention of 95.3% (Figure 5e). Additionally, the NTM system displays a smaller voltage drop during the static period (Figure S35, Supporting Information). These findings suggest that the NTM electrolyte effectively mitigates side reactions, likely due to the formation of a stable interfacial film that suppresses electrolyte decomposition.

XPS was further employed to investigate the interfacial layers of the NVP cathode and HC anode in the cycled full cells. As shown in Figure S36 (Supporting Information, NVP cathode side), the electrode cycled in the NTM electrolyte exhibits lower C and O elemental contents but higher Na and F elemental contents on the surface compared with the NP electrolyte. source_refs.raw_quote: The liquid temperature range of the electrolyte determines the battery's operational capability across a wide temperature range. Particularly at extremely low temperatures, the electrolyte's antifreezing properties are critical to ensuring battery operability. $^{[44]}$ Digital photographs show that the NTM electrolyte retains good fluidity without phase transition even when the temperature drops to $-60\ ^{\circ}C$ , thereby demonstrating superior anti-freezing properties (Figure S21, Supporting Information). Figures 4a and S22 (Supporting Information) show that the NP electrolyte shows a sharp decline in ionic conductivity below $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ due to the high viscosity of PC. In contrast, the NTM electrolyte exhibits superior ionic conductivity across the entire temperature range, particularly at sub-zero conditions, and exhibits lower activation energies for ion transport from $50\ ^{\circ}C$ to $-50\ ^{\circ}C$ (1.24 and 2.00 kJ mol $^{-1}$ vs. 2.00 and 3.04 kJ mol $^{-1}$ for NT vs. 2.32 and 4.91 kJ mol $^{-1}$ for NP). Notably, at $-40\ ^{\circ}C$ , the NTM electrolyte retains an ionic conductivity of 1.4 mS cm $^{-1}$ , significantly higher than those of NT (0.27 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) and NP (0.23 mS cm $^{-1}$ ), as detailed in Table S2 (Supporting Information).

citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

2.4. Electrochemical Performance of Full Cell
We also have tested the low-temperature performance of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL in the cathode material of SIBs. Na $_{3}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{3}$ was selected as the cathode with Na metal anode to assemble a coin cell. Rate performance of Na||NVP coupled with both electrolytes were evaluated. NVP paired with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL achieves a capacity of up to 74.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while it exclusively remains 60.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2, as demonstrated in Figures S22–S24 (Supporting Information). Surprisingly, it can operate normally at LT, and specifically preserve a capacity of 79.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ at $-40$ °C, which is equivalent to 80.0% of the capacity at 25 °C in Figure S25 (Supporting Information). This indicates that temperature-adaptive electrolytes are not only compatible with NVP, but can also upgrade the rate performance and low-temperature performance of NVP cathode.

To further verify the feasibility of electrolytes in SIBs, the coin full cell with NVP cathode and pre-cycled HC anode was assembled and subjected to rate performance testing at 25 °C. It displays that the full cell coupled with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can still retain a capacity of 71.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while the cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 can only bestow a capacity of 52.3 mAh g $^{-1}$ in Figure 6a. Additionally, the performance of the full cell was evaluated at -40 °C and it was manifested that the full cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can preserve 64.8% of its capacity at 25 °C in Figure 6b. After 50 cycles of 0.1 C (10 mA g $^{-1}$ ) at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 95.7%, and then after 50 cycles of 0.1 C at -40 °C, the capacity retention rate was 92.8%, as shown in Figure 6c. To test the practical application of electrolytes, a piece pouch cell (45 mAh) was assembled for cycling testing in Figure 6d and Figure S26 (Supporting Information). After cycling 100 cycles at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 86.7%. Then, the pouch cell was cycled 100 cycles at -30 °C, and the capacity retention rate was 92.43% in Figure 6e. Therefore, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL electrolyte with a temperature-adaptive solvent structure holds great potential in the practical application of SIBs.

citations.quote:
Yuewei Cui, Youxuan Ni, Yuankun Wang, Linyue Wang, Wenxuan Yang, Shuang Wu, Weiwei Xie, Kai Zhang, Zhenhua Yan,\* and Jun Chen\*

Sodium-ion batteries are applied to cold-resistant energy storage hindered by phase transitions and sluggish $Na^{+}$ migration of traditional carbonate-based electrolytes at low temperatures. The desolvation of $Na^{+}$ is a crucial step in impeding the transport of $Na^{+}$ , which primarily attributes to the robust solvent coordination of $Na^{+}$ . Herein, a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with an ultraweakly coordinated 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) is designed for constructing anion-rich solvation structure in a diglyme (G2)-based electrolyte. The electronegativity of the oxygen atoms of G2 is attenuated by dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2. As the temperature drops, the weakened $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) interaction leads to increased anionic coordination and less solvent coordination, facilitating the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ . This anionic-enhanced solvation structure contributes to the formation of stable solid electrolyte interface at the hard carbon (HC) anode, which accelerates $Na^{+}$ transport and diminishing the voltage polarization at low temperatures. Consequently, the HC anode can retain a high capacity of 203.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -50 °C, and the pouch cell composed of $HC||Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}$ at -30 °C achieves a capacity retention of 92.43% after 100 cycles at 0.1 C.

The desolvation of $Na^{+}$ is a crucial step in impeding the transport of $Na^{+}$ , which primarily attributes to the robust solvent coordination of $Na^{+}$ . Herein, a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with an ultraweakly coordinated 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) is designed for constructing anion-rich solvation structure in a diglyme (G2)-based electrolyte. The electronegativity of the oxygen atoms of G2 is attenuated by dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2. As the temperature drops, the weakened $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) interaction leads to increased anionic coordination and less solvent coordination, facilitating the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ . This anionic-enhanced solvation structure contributes to the formation of stable solid electrolyte interface at the hard carbon (HC) anode, which accelerates $Na^{+}$ transport and diminishing the voltage polarization at low temperatures. Consequently, the HC anode can retain a high capacity of 203.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -50 °C, and the pouch cell composed of $HC||Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}$ at -30 °C achieves a capacity retention of 92.43% after 100 cycles at 0.1 C.

The only residual gap is that no direct -40 °C, 100-cycle pouch-cell measurement is reported; this is a limited gap, not a contradiction, so the electrolyte is recommended for selection while noting that the -40 °C pouch combination remains to be confirmed.

citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

citations.quote: We also have tested the low-temperature performance of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL in the cathode material of SIBs. Na $_{3}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{3}$ was selected as the cathode with Na metal anode to assemble a coin cell. Rate performance of Na||NVP coupled with both electrolytes were evaluated. citations.quote: To quantitatively elucidate the solvation structure of the two electrolytes, classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed at 25 °C. The radial distribution function (RDF) in Figure 2e,f displays the distribution of each component around $Na^{+}$ in two electrolytes at 25 °C. The average coordination number (CN) values of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) in 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 and 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL are 5.979 and 4.733, respectively. The CN of Na–F ( $PF_{6}^{-}$ ) increases from 0.233 to 1.092, as shown in Figure 2g and Table S1 (Supporting Information). This indeed indicates that DOL weakens the coordination oxygen activity of G2, thereby reducing the coordination of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) and increasing the coordination of anions. The phase transition temperatures of the two electrolytes were evaluated by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and cryopolarizing microscope. Remarkably, the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is $-91$ °C, while the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 is only $-46$ °C, as shown in Figure 2h. Moreover, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 generates small ice crystals at $-50$ °C and emerges a large-scale phase transition at $-70$ °C. 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is a pure liquid at $-50$ °C and solvent crystallization does not occur until it is cooled to $-110$ °C (Figure S3, Supporting Information). Variable temperature viscosity tests were conducted on these two electrolytes in Figure 2i.

citations.quote: As the most commonly used electrolyte for SIBs, a PC-based electrolyte composed of 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ -PC/FEC was used as the control (hereafter referred to as PC) [42,43]. Similarly, the proposed carboxylate ester-based electrolytes in this work are composed of MP, FEC, and NaPF $_{6}$ . Firstly, the influence of concentration on electrochemical stability and ionic conductivity of the electrolyte was investigated, and as shown in Fig. S1(a), the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte with 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ is significantly higher than that of the electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ . Moreover, the MP-based electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ has better electrochemical stability (Fig. S1(b)), therefore 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ -MP/FEC was selected for research, which will be referred to as MP in the following. The redox reaction activities of isolated solvents and sodium salt of MP and PC-based electrolytes are investigated with frontier molecular orbital theory, involving the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy levels (Fig. 1(a)). The LUMO/HOMO energy level of MP is close to PC, which indicates MP has considerable oxidation/reduction stability compared to PC. In addition, the HOMO level of FEC is lower than that of the other solvents, indicating the stronger capability of the free fluorinated carbonate solvent against oxidation.

citations.quote: In summary, we designed a simple and efficient carboxylate ester-based electrolyte, using MP and FEC as the cosolvent in NVPOF instead of the most common PC-based electrolyte, which greatly enhances the low-temperature performance of the NVPOF cathode, mainly due to the enhanced ion conductivity and depressed electrode-electrolyte interface resistance. As a result, operating at $-25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF electrode with MP-based electrolyte can cycle for more than 500 cycles with a capacity of $82\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $1\mathrm{C}$ . Even at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF cathode still exhibits high-rate performance (50% capacity retention at $0.5\mathrm{C}$ ) and good cycling stability (96% capacity retention at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ after 100 cycles), reflecting the remarkable low-temperature performance of MP-based electrolyte. In addition, the low viscosity and freezing point of MP enable batteries to operate at temperatures as low as $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The homogeneous beneficial CEI formation and the fast kinetics of MP-based electrolytes at low temperatures were investigated by GITT and XPS tests, explaining the superiority of MP-based electrolytes as a low-temperature electrolyte compared to PC-based electrolytes. Additionally, the HC||NVPOF full cell has remarkable low-temperature performance as expected, delivering high initial discharge capacity of 108.4 and $73.0\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $-25$ and $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively.

citations.chunk_id: 0038_Liu 等 - 2024 - Ester-based anti-freezing electrolyte achieving ultra-low temperature cycling for sodium-ion batteri::sec11::child0
citations.quote: In summary, we designed a simple and efficient carboxylate ester-based electrolyte, using MP and FEC as the cosolvent in NVPOF instead of the most common PC-based electrolyte, which greatly enhances the low-temperature performance of the NVPOF cathode, mainly due to the enhanced ion conductivity and depressed electrode-electrolyte interface resistance. As a result, operating at $-25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF electrode with MP-based electrolyte can cycle for more than 500 cycles with a capacity of $82\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $1\mathrm{C}$ . Even at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF cathode still exhibits high-rate performance (50% capacity retention at $0.5\mathrm{C}$ ) and good cycling stability (96% capacity retention at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ after 100 cycles), reflecting the remarkable low-temperature performance of MP-based electrolyte. In addition, the low viscosity and freezing point of MP enable batteries to operate at temperatures as low as $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The homogeneous beneficial CEI formation and the fast kinetics of MP-based electrolytes at low temperatures were investigated by GITT and XPS tests, explaining the superiority of MP-based electrolytes as a low-temperature electrolyte compared to PC-based electrolytes. Additionally, the HC||NVPOF full cell has remarkable low-temperature performance as expected, delivering high initial discharge capacity of 108.4 and $73.0\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $-25$ and $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively.

citations.quote: The Na+-MP complex exhibits a low binding energy (-1.38 eV), consistent with its low DN value, further validating the weak coordination ability of MP. The redox behavior of the electrolyte was further evaluated using molecular orbital theory (Figure S3, Supporting Information). PF6− possesses the lowest highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level (-10.16 eV), indicating strong resistance to electron loss and enhanced oxidative stability. Moreover, its low lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) suggests preferential decomposition at the negative electrode, thereby improving interfacial compatibility with TEP. Based on optimizations in nonflammability, ionic conductivity and long cycle performance, the 2.0 M NaPF6 in TEP/MP +1 wt% VC (6:4 by volume ratio, denoted as NTM) is selected as the optimal electrolyte for further investigation (Figures S2 and S4, Supporting Information), with 2.0 M NaPF6 dissolved in TEP +1 wt% VC (denoted as NT) and traditional carbonate electrolyte 1.0 M NaPF6 in PC (denoted as NP) serving as control groups. Moreover, the NTM electrolyte not only exhibits a reduced contact angle with the separator (Figure S5, Supporting Information), indicative of decreased electrolyte viscosity and improved wettability, but also shows an oxidation potential of up to 4.52 V and a lower reduction potential (Figure S6, Supporting Information).

citations.quote: To further validate the practicality of the NTM electrolyte, full cells with NVP cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes were constructed, operating within the voltage range of 2.0–3.6 V (Figure 5a). The NVP||HC full cell, without any presodiation treatment, exhibits a high specific capacity of 88.0 mA h g $^{-1}$ and excellent cycling stability over 100 cycles at 50 mA g $^{-1}$ , maintaining an impressive capacity retention of 84.9% in the NTM electrolyte. This retention markedly surpasses that of the conventional NP electrolyte (51.9%), as illustrated in Figure 5b,c. Furthermore, the full cell utilizing the NTM electrolyte demonstrates superior rate capability, delivering reversible capacities of 87.2, 82.0, 79.1, 77.0, 71.9, and 68.1 mA h g $^{-1}$ at 20, 50, 80, 100, 200, and 300 mA g $^{-1}$ , respectively (Figure 5d). The charge–discharge curves exhibit minimal polarization even at elevated rates (Figure S32, Supporting Information). In addition, the overall electrical performance of the NTM electrolyte is better than that of the NED (NP-EC/DMC) electrolyte (Figure S33, Supporting Information). Notably, the NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 500 cycles at a high current of 200 mA g $^{-1}$ (Figure S34, Supporting Information). Self-discharge behavior was further evaluated in the NVP||HC full-cell system. The results display that the NP electrolyte system retains 72.8% of its discharge capacity after 48 h of rest (based on 4th cycle).

2.5. Toward Practical Viability
To further validate the practicality of the NTM electrolyte, full cells with NVP cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes were constructed, operating within the voltage range of 2.0–3.6 V (Figure 5a). The NVP||HC full cell, without any presodiation treatment, exhibits a high specific capacity of 88.0 mA h g $^{-1}$ and excellent cycling stability over 100 cycles at 50 mA g $^{-1}$ , maintaining an impressive capacity retention of 84.9% in the NTM electrolyte. This retention markedly surpasses that of the conventional NP electrolyte (51.9%), as illustrated in Figure 5b,c. Furthermore, the full cell utilizing the NTM electrolyte demonstrates superior rate capability, delivering reversible capacities of 87.2, 82.0, 79.1, 77.0, 71.9, and 68.1 mA h g $^{-1}$ at 20, 50, 80, 100, 200, and 300 mA g $^{-1}$ , respectively (Figure 5d). The charge–discharge curves exhibit minimal polarization even at elevated rates (Figure S32, Supporting Information). In addition, the overall electrical performance of the NTM electrolyte is better than that of the NED (NP-EC/DMC) electrolyte (Figure S33, Supporting Information). Notably, the NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 500 cycles at a high current of 200 mA g $^{-1}$ (Figure S34, Supporting Information). Self-discharge behavior was further evaluated in the NVP||HC full-cell system. The results display that the NP electrolyte system retains 72.8% of its discharge capacity after 48 h of rest (based on 4th cycle). In contrast, the NTM system exhibits a smaller capacity loss, achieving a retention of 95.3% (Figure 5e). Additionally, the NTM system displays a smaller voltage drop during the static period (Figure S35, Supporting Information). These findings suggest that the NTM electrolyte effectively mitigates side reactions, likely due to the formation of a stable interfacial film that suppresses electrolyte decomposition.

citations.quote: The liquid temperature range of the electrolyte determines the battery's operational capability across a wide temperature range. Particularly at extremely low temperatures, the electrolyte's antifreezing properties are critical to ensuring battery operability. $^{[44]}$ Digital photographs show that the NTM electrolyte retains good fluidity without phase transition even when the temperature drops to $-60\ ^{\circ}C$ , thereby demonstrating superior anti-freezing properties (Figure S21, Supporting Information). Figures 4a and S22 (Supporting Information) show that the NP electrolyte shows a sharp decline in ionic conductivity below $-30\ ^{\circ}C$ due to the high viscosity of PC. In contrast, the NTM electrolyte exhibits superior ionic conductivity across the entire temperature range, particularly at sub-zero conditions, and exhibits lower activation energies for ion transport from $50\ ^{\circ}C$ to $-50\ ^{\circ}C$ (1.24 and 2.00 kJ mol $^{-1}$ vs. 2.00 and 3.04 kJ mol $^{-1}$ for NT vs. 2.32 and 4.91 kJ mol $^{-1}$ for NP). Notably, at $-40\ ^{\circ}C$ , the NTM electrolyte retains an ionic conductivity of 1.4 mS cm $^{-1}$ , significantly higher than those of NT (0.27 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) and NP (0.23 mS cm $^{-1}$ ), as detailed in Table S2 (Supporting Information).

citations.quote: This enhanced stability primarily arises from the formation of NaF-enriched gradient CEI/SEI layers, which effectively suppress electrolyte decomposition at elevated temperatures. In addition, the NVP||HC full cell employing the NTM electrolyte maintains stable cycling for 100 cycles under the extreme conditions of high voltage (4.3 V) and 50 °C (Figure S42, Supporting Information). The NVP||HC full cell with the NTM electrolyte exhibits remarkable temperature adaptability across a broad temperature range. At low temperatures of -20 and -40 °C, the NTM-based electrolyte still delivers high discharge capacities of 71.5 mA h g $^{-1}$ and 62.2 mA h g $^{-1}$ , corresponding to 83.2% and 72.4% of the discharge capacity at room temperature, respectively (Figure 5g). Additionally, the battery can stably complete 50 discharge cycles at -20 °C (Figure S43, Supporting Information), and even successfully operate for 20 cycles at -40 °C, maintaining a capacity retention rate of 83.9% (Figure 5h; Figure S44, Supporting Information). Benefiting from the excellent anti-freezing capability and low-temperature ionic conductivity of the NTM electrolyte, the NVP||HC full cell delivers an average specific capacity of 31.8 mA h g $^{-1}$ at -60 °C (Figure S45, Supporting Information).

association_citations.quote: The Na+-MP complex exhibits a low binding energy (-1.38 eV), consistent with its low DN value, further validating the weak coordination ability of MP. The redox behavior of the electrolyte was further evaluated using molecular orbital theory (Figure S3, Supporting Information). PF6− possesses the lowest highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level (-10.16 eV), indicating strong resistance to electron loss and enhanced oxidative stability. Moreover, its low lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) suggests preferential decomposition at the negative electrode, thereby improving interfacial compatibility with TEP. Based on optimizations in nonflammability, ionic conductivity and long cycle performance, the 2.0 M NaPF6 in TEP/MP +1 wt% VC (6:4 by volume ratio, denoted as NTM) is selected as the optimal electrolyte for further investigation (Figures S2 and S4, Supporting Information), with 2.0 M NaPF6 dissolved in TEP +1 wt% VC (denoted as NT) and traditional carbonate electrolyte 1.0 M NaPF6 in PC (denoted as NP) serving as control groups. Moreover, the NTM electrolyte not only exhibits a reduced contact angle with the separator (Figure S5, Supporting Information), indicative of decreased electrolyte viscosity and improved wettability, but also shows an oxidation potential of up to 4.52 V and a lower reduction potential (Figure S6, Supporting Information).

citations.quote: As depicted in Fig. 5a, the NTP||NVP full cell demonstrated the specific capacity of 108 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 105 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 and 0 °C, respectively. Even the test temperature decreased to -40 °C, the full cell still maintained a reversible capacity of 75 mAh g $^{-1}$ , approximately 64 % of the capacity than it at room temperature. This impressive performance can be attributed to the low freezing point of ether-based electrolytes, enabling normal operation and high capacity at -40 °C. Despite some polarization at low temperatures, the discharge plateau of the NTP anode remains above -40 °C, effectively preventing sodium precipitation and ensuring safe cell operation. The cycling stability and rate capacity of the NTP||NVP cell at -40 °C were also assessed. As shown in Fig. 5b, the cell exhibited a remarkable rate capacity at -40 °C, retaining 72 % capacity from 0.1 to 1 C. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

evidence_ledger.quote:
Yuewei Cui, Youxuan Ni, Yuankun Wang, Linyue Wang, Wenxuan Yang, Shuang Wu, Weiwei Xie, Kai Zhang, Zhenhua Yan,\* and Jun Chen\*

Sodium-ion batteries are applied to cold-resistant energy storage hindered by phase transitions and sluggish $Na^{+}$ migration of traditional carbonate-based electrolytes at low temperatures. The desolvation of $Na^{+}$ is a crucial step in impeding the transport of $Na^{+}$ , which primarily attributes to the robust solvent coordination of $Na^{+}$ . Herein, a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with an ultraweakly coordinated 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) is designed for constructing anion-rich solvation structure in a diglyme (G2)-based electrolyte. The electronegativity of the oxygen atoms of G2 is attenuated by dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2. As the temperature drops, the weakened $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) interaction leads to increased anionic coordination and less solvent coordination, facilitating the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ . This anionic-enhanced solvation structure contributes to the formation of stable solid electrolyte interface at the hard carbon (HC) anode, which accelerates $Na^{+}$ transport and diminishing the voltage polarization at low temperatures. Consequently, the HC anode can retain a high capacity of 203.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -50 °C, and the pouch cell composed of $HC||Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}$ at -30 °C achieves a capacity retention of 92.43% after 100 cycles at 0.1 C.

evidence_ledger.quote: In summary, we designed a simple and efficient carboxylate ester-based electrolyte, using MP and FEC as the cosolvent in NVPOF instead of the most common PC-based electrolyte, which greatly enhances the low-temperature performance of the NVPOF cathode, mainly due to the enhanced ion conductivity and depressed electrode-electrolyte interface resistance. As a result, operating at $-25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF electrode with MP-based electrolyte can cycle for more than 500 cycles with a capacity of $82\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $1\mathrm{C}$ . Even at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF cathode still exhibits high-rate performance (50% capacity retention at $0.5\mathrm{C}$ ) and good cycling stability (96% capacity retention at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ after 100 cycles), reflecting the remarkable low-temperature performance of MP-based electrolyte. In addition, the low viscosity and freezing point of MP enable batteries to operate at temperatures as low as $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The homogeneous beneficial CEI formation and the fast kinetics of MP-based electrolytes at low temperatures were investigated by GITT and XPS tests, explaining the superiority of MP-based electrolytes as a low-temperature electrolyte compared to PC-based electrolytes. Additionally, the HC||NVPOF full cell has remarkable low-temperature performance as expected, delivering high initial discharge capacity of 108.4 and $73.0\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $-25$ and $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively.

The redox behavior of the electrolyte was further evaluated using molecular orbital theory (Figure S3, Supporting Information). PF6− possesses the lowest highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level (-10.16 eV), indicating strong resistance to electron loss and enhanced oxidative stability. Moreover, its low lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) suggests preferential decomposition at the negative electrode, thereby improving interfacial compatibility with TEP. Based on optimizations in nonflammability, ionic conductivity and long cycle performance, the 2.0 M NaPF6 in TEP/MP +1 wt% VC (6:4 by volume ratio, denoted as NTM) is selected as the optimal electrolyte for further investigation (Figures S2 and S4, Supporting Information), with 2.0 M NaPF6 dissolved in TEP +1 wt% VC (denoted as NT) and traditional carbonate electrolyte 1.0 M NaPF6 in PC (denoted as NP) serving as control groups. Moreover, the NTM electrolyte not only exhibits a reduced contact angle with the separator (Figure S5, Supporting Information), indicative of decreased electrolyte viscosity and improved wettability, but also shows an oxidation potential of up to 4.52 V and a lower reduction potential (Figure S6, Supporting Information).

evidence_ledger.quote: To quantitatively elucidate the solvation structure of the two electrolytes, classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed at 25 °C. The radial distribution function (RDF) in Figure 2e,f displays the distribution of each component around $Na^{+}$ in two electrolytes at 25 °C. The average coordination number (CN) values of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) in 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 and 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL are 5.979 and 4.733, respectively. The CN of Na–F ( $PF_{6}^{-}$ ) increases from 0.233 to 1.092, as shown in Figure 2g and Table S1 (Supporting Information). This indeed indicates that DOL weakens the coordination oxygen activity of G2, thereby reducing the coordination of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) and increasing the coordination of anions. The phase transition temperatures of the two electrolytes were evaluated by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and cryopolarizing microscope. Remarkably, the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is $-91$ °C, while the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 is only $-46$ °C, as shown in Figure 2h. Moreover, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 generates small ice crystals at $-50$ °C and emerges a large-scale phase transition at $-70$ °C. 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is a pure liquid at $-50$ °C and solvent crystallization does not occur until it is cooled to $-110$ °C (Figure S3, Supporting Information). Variable temperature viscosity tests were conducted on these two electrolytes in Figure 2i.

evidence_ledger.quote: As the most commonly used electrolyte for SIBs, a PC-based electrolyte composed of 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ -PC/FEC was used as the control (hereafter referred to as PC) [42,43]. Firstly, the influence of concentration on electrochemical stability and ionic conductivity of the electrolyte was investigated, and as shown in Fig. S1(a), the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte with 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ is significantly higher than that of the electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ . Moreover, the MP-based electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ has better electrochemical stability (Fig. S1(b)), therefore 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ -MP/FEC was selected for research, which will be referred to as MP in the following. The redox reaction activities of isolated solvents and sodium salt of MP and PC-based electrolytes are investigated with frontier molecular orbital theory, involving the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy levels (Fig. 1(a)). The LUMO/HOMO energy level of MP is close to PC, which indicates MP has considerable oxidation/reduction stability compared to PC. In addition, the HOMO level of FEC is lower than that of the other solvents, indicating the stronger capability of the free fluorinated carbonate solvent against oxidation.

In addition, the overall electrical performance of the NTM electrolyte is better than that of the NED (NP-EC/DMC) electrolyte (Figure S33, Supporting Information). citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

2.4. Electrochemical Performance of Full Cell
We also have tested the low-temperature performance of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL in the cathode material of SIBs. Na $_{3}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{3}$ was selected as the cathode with Na metal anode to assemble a coin cell. Rate performance of Na||NVP coupled with both electrolytes were evaluated. NVP paired with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL achieves a capacity of up to 74.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while it exclusively remains 60.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2, as demonstrated in Figures S22–S24 (Supporting Information). Surprisingly, it can operate normally at LT, and specifically preserve a capacity of 79.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ at $-40$ °C, which is equivalent to 80.0% of the capacity at 25 °C in Figure S25 (Supporting Information). This indicates that temperature-adaptive electrolytes are not only compatible with NVP, but can also upgrade the rate performance and low-temperature performance of NVP cathode.

To further verify the feasibility of electrolytes in SIBs, the coin full cell with NVP cathode and pre-cycled HC anode was assembled and subjected to rate performance testing at 25 °C. It displays that the full cell coupled with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can still retain a capacity of 71.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while the cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 can only bestow a capacity of 52.3 mAh g $^{-1}$ in Figure 6a. citations.quote:
Yuewei Cui, Youxuan Ni, Yuankun Wang, Linyue Wang, Wenxuan Yang, Shuang Wu, Weiwei Xie, Kai Zhang, Zhenhua Yan,\* and Jun Chen\*

Sodium-ion batteries are applied to cold-resistant energy storage hindered by phase transitions and sluggish $Na^{+}$ migration of traditional carbonate-based electrolytes at low temperatures. The desolvation of $Na^{+}$ is a crucial step in impeding the transport of $Na^{+}$ , which primarily attributes to the robust solvent coordination of $Na^{+}$ . Herein, a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with an ultraweakly coordinated 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) is designed for constructing anion-rich solvation structure in a diglyme (G2)-based electrolyte. The electronegativity of the oxygen atoms of G2 is attenuated by dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2. As the temperature drops, the weakened $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) interaction leads to increased anionic coordination and less solvent coordination, facilitating the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ . This anionic-enhanced solvation structure contributes to the formation of stable solid electrolyte interface at the hard carbon (HC) anode, which accelerates $Na^{+}$ transport and diminishing the voltage polarization at low temperatures. Consequently, the HC anode can retain a high capacity of 203.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -50 °C, and the pouch cell composed of $HC||Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}$ at -30 °C achieves a capacity retention of 92.43% after 100 cycles at 0.1 C.

association_citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

citations.chunk_id: 0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec2::child4
citations.quote: To quantitatively elucidate the solvation structure of the two electrolytes, classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed at 25 °C. The radial distribution function (RDF) in Figure 2e,f displays the distribution of each component around $Na^{+}$ in two electrolytes at 25 °C. The average coordination number (CN) values of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) in 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 and 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL are 5.979 and 4.733, respectively. The CN of Na–F ( $PF_{6}^{-}$ ) increases from 0.233 to 1.092, as shown in Figure 2g and Table S1 (Supporting Information). This indeed indicates that DOL weakens the coordination oxygen activity of G2, thereby reducing the coordination of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) and increasing the coordination of anions. The phase transition temperatures of the two electrolytes were evaluated by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and cryopolarizing microscope. Remarkably, the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is $-91$ °C, while the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 is only $-46$ °C, as shown in Figure 2h. Moreover, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 generates small ice crystals at $-50$ °C and emerges a large-scale phase transition at $-70$ °C. 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is a pure liquid at $-50$ °C and solvent crystallization does not occur until it is cooled to $-110$ °C (Figure S3, Supporting Information). Variable temperature viscosity tests were conducted on these two electrolytes in Figure 2i.

citations.chunk_id: 0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec2::child5
citations.quote: Variable temperature viscosity tests were conducted on these two electrolytes in Figure 2i. Unlike the viscosity of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2, which rises dramatically with decreasing temperatures, the viscosity of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL bestows a slightly growth trend. Simultaneously, the ionic conductivity (IC) of the electrolytes was calculated based on the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements at different temperatures, as shown in Figure 2j. Apparently, 0.5 M NaPF $_6$ G2/DOL maintains a higher ionic conductivity which is less affected by temperature. Especially, the ionic conductivity of 0.5 M NaPF $_6$ G2 and 0.5 M NaPF $_6$ G2/DOL is 0.49 and 3.39 mS cm $^{-1}$ at $-50$ °C, respectively.

association_citations.chunk_id: 0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec5::child0
association_citations.quote: We also have tested the low-temperature performance of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL in the cathode material of SIBs. Na $_{3}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{3}$ was selected as the cathode with Na metal anode to assemble a coin cell. Rate performance of Na||NVP coupled with both electrolytes were evaluated. NVP paired with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL achieves a capacity of up to 74.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while it exclusively remains 60.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2, as demonstrated in Figures S22–S24 (Supporting Information). Surprisingly, it can operate normally at LT, and specifically preserve a capacity of 79.8 mAh g $^{-1}$ at $-40$ °C, which is equivalent to 80.0% of the capacity at 25 °C in Figure S25 (Supporting Information). This indicates that temperature-adaptive electrolytes are not only compatible with NVP, but can also upgrade the rate performance and low-temperature performance of NVP cathode. To further verify the feasibility of electrolytes in SIBs, the coin full cell with NVP cathode and pre-cycled HC anode was assembled and subjected to rate performance testing at 25 °C. It displays that the full cell coupled with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can still retain a capacity of 71.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while the cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 can only bestow a capacity of 52.3 mAh g $^{-1}$ in Figure 6a.

association_citations.chunk_id: 0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec5::child1
association_citations.quote: Additionally, the performance of the full cell was evaluated at -40 °C and it was manifested that the full cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can preserve 64.8% of its capacity at 25 °C in Figure 6b. After 50 cycles of 0.1 C (10 mA g $^{-1}$ ) at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 95.7%, and then after 50 cycles of 0.1 C at -40 °C, the capacity retention rate was 92.8%, as shown in Figure 6c. To test the practical application of electrolytes, a piece pouch cell (45 mAh) was assembled for cycling testing in Figure 6d and Figure S26 (Supporting Information). After cycling 100 cycles at 25 °C, the capacity retention rate was 86.7%. Then, the pouch cell was cycled 100 cycles at -30 °C, and the capacity retention rate was 92.43% in Figure 6e. Therefore, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL electrolyte with a temperature-adaptive solvent structure holds great potential in the practical application of SIBs. Additionally, the temperature-adapted solvation structure may widespreadly exist in G2/DOL derivative electrolytes. We have tested the low-temperature performance of G2/THF, DME/DOL and DME/THF based electrolytes, as shown in Figure S27 (Supporting Information). HC can still retain 242.5 mAh g $^{-1}$ , 243.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 247.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ in G2/THF, DME/DOL and DME/THF based electrolytes at -40 °C, with capacity retention rates of 95.71%, 95.41% and 95.44% after 200 cycles, respectively.

citations.quote: As the most commonly used electrolyte for SIBs, a PC-based electrolyte composed of 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ -PC/FEC was used as the control (hereafter referred to as PC) [42,43]. Similarly, the proposed carboxylate ester-based electrolytes in this work are composed of MP, FEC, and NaPF $_{6}$ . Firstly, the influence of concentration on electrochemical stability and ionic conductivity of the electrolyte was investigated, and as shown in Fig. S1(a), the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte with 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ is significantly higher than that of the electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ . Moreover, the MP-based electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ has better electrochemical stability (Fig. S1(b)), therefore 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ -MP/FEC was selected for research, which will be referred to as MP in the following. The redox reaction activities of isolated solvents and sodium salt of MP and PC-based electrolytes are investigated with frontier molecular orbital theory, involving the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy levels (Fig. 1(a)). The LUMO/HOMO energy level of MP is close to PC, which indicates MP has considerable oxidation/reduction stability compared to PC. In addition, the HOMO level of FEC is lower than that of the other solvents, indicating the stronger capability of the free fluorinated carbonate solvent against oxidation.

citations.chunk_id: 0038_Liu 等 - 2024 - Ester-based anti-freezing electrolyte achieving ultra-low temperature cycling for sodium-ion batteri::sec11::child0
citations.quote: In summary, we designed a simple and efficient carboxylate ester-based electrolyte, using MP and FEC as the cosolvent in NVPOF instead of the most common PC-based electrolyte, which greatly enhances the low-temperature performance of the NVPOF cathode, mainly due to the enhanced ion conductivity and depressed electrode-electrolyte interface resistance. As a result, operating at $-25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF electrode with MP-based electrolyte can cycle for more than 500 cycles with a capacity of $82\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $1\mathrm{C}$ . Even at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF cathode still exhibits high-rate performance (50% capacity retention at $0.5\mathrm{C}$ ) and good cycling stability (96% capacity retention at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ after 100 cycles), reflecting the remarkable low-temperature performance of MP-based electrolyte. In addition, the low viscosity and freezing point of MP enable batteries to operate at temperatures as low as $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The homogeneous beneficial CEI formation and the fast kinetics of MP-based electrolytes at low temperatures were investigated by GITT and XPS tests, explaining the superiority of MP-based electrolytes as a low-temperature electrolyte compared to PC-based electrolytes. Additionally, the HC||NVPOF full cell has remarkable low-temperature performance as expected, delivering high initial discharge capacity of 108.4 and $73.0\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $-25$ and $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively.

To further validate the practicality of the NTM electrolyte, full cells with NVP cathodes and hard carbon (HC) anodes were constructed, operating within the voltage range of 2.0–3.6 V (Figure 5a). At -40 °C, the NVP||Na cell with NP electrolyte delivers only 22.8 mA h g $^{-1}$ after 100 cycles at 50 mA g $^{-1}$ , owing to its low ionic conductivity and sluggish ion transport. The NT-based cell fails rapidly due to partial electrolyte solidification and high ion transfer activation energy (Figure 4b). Conversely, the NVP||Na cell with NTM electrolyte delivers 64.8 mA h g $^{-1}$ and 95.6% capacity retention after 100 cycles (Figure 4d,e; Figure S27, Supporting Information), underscoring its superior competitiveness (Table S4, Supporting Information). citations.quote: As depicted in Fig. 5a, the NTP||NVP full cell demonstrated the specific capacity of 108 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 105 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 and 0 °C, respectively. Even the test temperature decreased to -40 °C, the full cell still maintained a reversible capacity of 75 mAh g $^{-1}$ , approximately 64 % of the capacity than it at room temperature. This impressive performance can be attributed to the low freezing point of ether-based electrolytes, enabling normal operation and high capacity at -40 °C. Despite some polarization at low temperatures, the discharge plateau of the NTP anode remains above -40 °C, effectively preventing sodium precipitation and ensuring safe cell operation. The cycling stability and rate capacity of the NTP||NVP cell at -40 °C were also assessed. As shown in Fig. 5b, the cell exhibited a remarkable rate capacity at -40 °C, retaining 72 % capacity from 0.1 to 1 C. Fig. 5c shows the cycle stability of NTP||NVP full cell, which demonstrates an excellent 93.1 % capacity retention after 180 cycles at 0.1 C. Following the high/low-temperature performance evaluation, we examined the high-temperature stability of the NTP||NVP cell from 30 to 60 °C. The constant-current charge/discharge curves in Fig. 5d indicate discharge capacities of 104.6, 108, and 112.2 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 30, 40, and 50 °C, respectively. Even at 60 °C, the cell delivered a reversible discharge specific capacity of 112.4 mAh g $^{-1}$ with an average coulombic efficiency of more than 99 %.

The ether-based electrolyte exhibits a gentler solvation energy change over a wide temperature range, and this temperature-adapted solvated structure with stabilized complexes can achieve higher Na-ion mobility at low temperatures, which helps to prevent the precipitation of Na.

Despite some polarization at low temperatures, the discharge plateau of the NTP anode remains above -40 °C, effectively preventing sodium precipitation and ensuring safe cell operation. The cycling stability and rate capacity of the NTP||NVP cell at -40 °C were also assessed. As shown in Fig. 5b, the cell exhibited a remarkable rate capacity at -40 °C, retaining 72 % capacity from 0.1 to 1 C. citations.chunk_id: 0009_Cui 等 - 2025 - A Temperature-Adapted Ultraweakly Solvating Electrolyte for Cold-Resistant Sodium-Ion Batteries::sec2::child0
citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

We also have tested the low-temperature performance of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL in the cathode material of SIBs. Na $_{3}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{3}$ was selected as the cathode with Na metal anode to assemble a coin cell. Rate performance of Na||NVP coupled with both electrolytes were evaluated. NVP paired with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL achieves a capacity of up to 74.7 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while it exclusively remains 60.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2, as demonstrated in Figures S22–S24 (Supporting Information). citations.quote:
Yuewei Cui, Youxuan Ni, Yuankun Wang, Linyue Wang, Wenxuan Yang, Shuang Wu, Weiwei Xie, Kai Zhang, Zhenhua Yan,\* and Jun Chen\*

Sodium-ion batteries are applied to cold-resistant energy storage hindered by phase transitions and sluggish $Na^{+}$ migration of traditional carbonate-based electrolytes at low temperatures. The desolvation of $Na^{+}$ is a crucial step in impeding the transport of $Na^{+}$ , which primarily attributes to the robust solvent coordination of $Na^{+}$ . Herein, a low-temperature adaptive electrolyte with an ultraweakly coordinated 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) is designed for constructing anion-rich solvation structure in a diglyme (G2)-based electrolyte. The electronegativity of the oxygen atoms of G2 is attenuated by dipole-dipole interaction between DOL and G2. As the temperature drops, the weakened $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) interaction leads to increased anionic coordination and less solvent coordination, facilitating the desolvation of $Na^{+}$ . This anionic-enhanced solvation structure contributes to the formation of stable solid electrolyte interface at the hard carbon (HC) anode, which accelerates $Na^{+}$ transport and diminishing the voltage polarization at low temperatures. Consequently, the HC anode can retain a high capacity of 203.9 mAh g $^{-1}$ (1 C) at -50 °C, and the pouch cell composed of $HC||Na_{3}V_{2}(PO_{4})_{3}$ at -30 °C achieves a capacity retention of 92.43% after 100 cycles at 0.1 C.

citations.quote: Primarily, $Na^{+}-O$ (DOL) has a lower binding energy compared to $Na^{+}-O$ (G2), as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, $Na^{+}$ can form a stable five-membered chelation structure with the negative-charged multidentate oxygen of G2 molecules. This endows the G2-based electrolyte high ionic conductivity, but regretfully, impedes $Na^{+}$ desolvation. DOL is a low polarity and low melting point ( $-95\ ^{\circ}C$ ) cyclic ether that exhibits dipole-dipole interactions with G2. Explicitly, ${}^{1}H$ and ${}^{17}O$ nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) were studied in Figure 2b; Figure S1 (Supporting Information). ${}^{1}H$ (G2) displays an upfield chemical shift in G2/DOL than G2, while the chemical shift of the ${}^{17}O$ (G2) shifts downfield. This implies that the dipole-dipole interactions between G2 and DOL weaken the shielding effect of electron clouds of O (G2) on atomic nucleus, indicating a decrease in the electron cloud density of O (G2). This demonstrates that DOL attenuates the electronegativity of donor O (G2), thereby diminishing the coordination of G2. $^{[16]}$ Consequently, DOL was blended into 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 with a volume ratio of 3:1 to prepare 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL for the low-temperature adaptive electrolyte. 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 as the reference electrolyte was compared and analyzed.

citations.quote: We also have tested the low-temperature performance of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL in the cathode material of SIBs. Na $_{3}$ V $_{2}$ (PO $_{4}$ ) $_{3}$ was selected as the cathode with Na metal anode to assemble a coin cell. Rate performance of Na||NVP coupled with both electrolytes were evaluated. To further verify the feasibility of electrolytes in SIBs, the coin full cell with NVP cathode and pre-cycled HC anode was assembled and subjected to rate performance testing at 25 °C. It displays that the full cell coupled with 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL can still retain a capacity of 71.6 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 C, while the cell using 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 can only bestow a capacity of 52.3 mAh g $^{-1}$ in Figure 6a.

citations.quote: To quantitatively elucidate the solvation structure of the two electrolytes, classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed at 25 °C. The radial distribution function (RDF) in Figure 2e,f displays the distribution of each component around $Na^{+}$ in two electrolytes at 25 °C. The average coordination number (CN) values of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) in 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2 and 0.5 M $NaPF_{6}$ G2/DOL are 5.979 and 4.733, respectively. The CN of Na–F ( $PF_{6}^{-}$ ) increases from 0.233 to 1.092, as shown in Figure 2g and Table S1 (Supporting Information). This indeed indicates that DOL weakens the coordination oxygen activity of G2, thereby reducing the coordination of $Na^{+}-O$ (G2) and increasing the coordination of anions. The phase transition temperatures of the two electrolytes were evaluated by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and cryopolarizing microscope. Remarkably, the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is $-91$ °C, while the melting point of 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 is only $-46$ °C, as shown in Figure 2h. Moreover, 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2 generates small ice crystals at $-50$ °C and emerges a large-scale phase transition at $-70$ °C. 0.5 M NaPF $_{6}$ G2/DOL is a pure liquid at $-50$ °C and solvent crystallization does not occur until it is cooled to $-110$ °C (Figure S3, Supporting Information). Variable temperature viscosity tests were conducted on these two electrolytes in Figure 2i.

citations.quote: As the most commonly used electrolyte for SIBs, a PC-based electrolyte composed of 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ -PC/FEC was used as the control (hereafter referred to as PC) [42,43]. Similarly, the proposed carboxylate ester-based electrolytes in this work are composed of MP, FEC, and NaPF $_{6}$ . Firstly, the influence of concentration on electrochemical stability and ionic conductivity of the electrolyte was investigated, and as shown in Fig. S1(a), the ionic conductivity of the electrolyte with 1 M NaPF $_{6}$ is significantly higher than that of the electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ . Moreover, the MP-based electrolyte with 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ has better electrochemical stability (Fig. S1(b)), therefore 2 M NaPF $_{6}$ -MP/FEC was selected for research, which will be referred to as MP in the following. The redox reaction activities of isolated solvents and sodium salt of MP and PC-based electrolytes are investigated with frontier molecular orbital theory, involving the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy levels (Fig. 1(a)). The LUMO/HOMO energy level of MP is close to PC, which indicates MP has considerable oxidation/reduction stability compared to PC. In addition, the HOMO level of FEC is lower than that of the other solvents, indicating the stronger capability of the free fluorinated carbonate solvent against oxidation.

citations.chunk_id: 0038_Liu 等 - 2024 - Ester-based anti-freezing electrolyte achieving ultra-low temperature cycling for sodium-ion batteri::sec11::child0
citations.quote: In summary, we designed a simple and efficient carboxylate ester-based electrolyte, using MP and FEC as the cosolvent in NVPOF instead of the most common PC-based electrolyte, which greatly enhances the low-temperature performance of the NVPOF cathode, mainly due to the enhanced ion conductivity and depressed electrode-electrolyte interface resistance. As a result, operating at $-25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF electrode with MP-based electrolyte can cycle for more than 500 cycles with a capacity of $82\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $1\mathrm{C}$ . Even at $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the NVPOF cathode still exhibits high-rate performance (50% capacity retention at $0.5\mathrm{C}$ ) and good cycling stability (96% capacity retention at $0.1\mathrm{C}$ after 100 cycles), reflecting the remarkable low-temperature performance of MP-based electrolyte. In addition, the low viscosity and freezing point of MP enable batteries to operate at temperatures as low as $-50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . The homogeneous beneficial CEI formation and the fast kinetics of MP-based electrolytes at low temperatures were investigated by GITT and XPS tests, explaining the superiority of MP-based electrolytes as a low-temperature electrolyte compared to PC-based electrolytes. Additionally, the HC||NVPOF full cell has remarkable low-temperature performance as expected, delivering high initial discharge capacity of 108.4 and $73.0\mathrm{mAhg^{-1}}$ at $-25$ and $-40^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively.

The redox behavior of the electrolyte was further evaluated using molecular orbital theory (Figure S3, Supporting Information). PF6− possesses the lowest highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level (-10.16 eV), indicating strong resistance to electron loss and enhanced oxidative stability. Moreover, its low lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) suggests preferential decomposition at the negative electrode, thereby improving interfacial compatibility with TEP. Based on optimizations in nonflammability, ionic conductivity and long cycle performance, the 2.0 M NaPF6 in TEP/MP +1 wt% VC (6:4 by volume ratio, denoted as NTM) is selected as the optimal electrolyte for further investigation (Figures S2 and S4, Supporting Information), with 2.0 M NaPF6 dissolved in TEP +1 wt% VC (denoted as NT) and traditional carbonate electrolyte 1.0 M NaPF6 in PC (denoted as NP) serving as control groups. Moreover, the NTM electrolyte not only exhibits a reduced contact angle with the separator (Figure S5, Supporting Information), indicative of decreased electrolyte viscosity and improved wettability, but also shows an oxidation potential of up to 4.52 V and a lower reduction potential (Figure S6, Supporting Information).

association_citations.quote: The Na+-MP complex exhibits a low binding energy (-1.38 eV), consistent with its low DN value, further validating the weak coordination ability of MP. The redox behavior of the electrolyte was further evaluated using molecular orbital theory (Figure S3, Supporting Information). PF6− possesses the lowest highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level (-10.16 eV), indicating strong resistance to electron loss and enhanced oxidative stability. Moreover, its low lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) suggests preferential decomposition at the negative electrode, thereby improving interfacial compatibility with TEP. Based on optimizations in nonflammability, ionic conductivity and long cycle performance, the 2.0 M NaPF6 in TEP/MP +1 wt% VC (6:4 by volume ratio, denoted as NTM) is selected as the optimal electrolyte for further investigation (Figures S2 and S4, Supporting Information), with 2.0 M NaPF6 dissolved in TEP +1 wt% VC (denoted as NT) and traditional carbonate electrolyte 1.0 M NaPF6 in PC (denoted as NP) serving as control groups. Moreover, the NTM electrolyte not only exhibits a reduced contact angle with the separator (Figure S5, Supporting Information), indicative of decreased electrolyte viscosity and improved wettability, but also shows an oxidation potential of up to 4.52 V and a lower reduction potential (Figure S6, Supporting Information).

citations.quote: As depicted in Fig. 5a, the NTP||NVP full cell demonstrated the specific capacity of 108 mAh g $^{-1}$ and 105 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 10 and 0 °C, respectively. Even the test temperature decreased to -40 °C, the full cell still maintained a reversible capacity of 75 mAh g $^{-1}$ , approximately 64 % of the capacity than it at room temperature. This impressive performance can be attributed to the low freezing point of ether-based electrolytes, enabling normal operation and high capacity at -40 °C. Despite some polarization at low temperatures, the discharge plateau of the NTP anode remains above -40 °C, effectively preventing sodium precipitation and ensuring safe cell operation. The cycling stability and rate capacity of the NTP||NVP cell at -40 °C were also assessed. As shown in Fig. 5b, the cell exhibited a remarkable rate capacity at -40 °C, retaining 72 % capacity from 0.1 to 1 C. Fig. 5c shows the cycle stability of NTP||NVP full cell, which demonstrates an excellent 93.1 % capacity retention after 180 cycles at 0.1 C. Following the high/low-temperature performance evaluation, we examined the high-temperature stability of the NTP||NVP cell from 30 to 60 °C. The constant-current charge/discharge curves in Fig. 5d indicate discharge capacities of 104.6, 108, and 112.2 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 30, 40, and 50 °C, respectively. Even at 60 °C, the cell delivered a reversible discharge specific capacity of 112.4 mAh g $^{-1}$ with an average coulombic efficiency of more than 99 %.
